1.overview: Loops are control-flow structures that repeat a block of code while a condition holds (for/while) or for a fixed count (for). Their primary purpose is iteration — executing the same logic multiple times without duplicating source lines. Variable declaration, function definition, and exception handling are separate language features with different roles.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "To declare variables". "To declare variables" sounds plausible but is wrong because variable declaration happens once with assignment or type declarations; loops consume variables but do not create them as their primary purpose.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "To execute a block of code repeatedly". "To execute a block of code repeatedly" is correct because this is the defining behavior of every loop construct — for, while, do-while — in all mainstream languages.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "To define a function". "To define a function" sounds plausible but is wrong because functions group reusable code; loops call code repeatedly inside an existing block but do not define named callable units.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "To handle exceptions". "To handle exceptions" sounds plausible but is wrong because try/catch (or try/except) blocks handle runtime errors; loops control repetition, not error recovery.

1.studyTip: Loop = repeat; if = branch; function = reuse; try = errors.

2.overview: In C, the `/` operator performs integer division when both operands are integers. 5 / 2 discards the fractional part (truncates toward zero), yielding 2 — not 2.5. To get floating-point division you need at least one operand as float/double (e.g., 5.0 / 2). printf("%d", ...) expects an integer format specifier.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "2.5". "2.5" sounds plausible but is wrong because 2.5 is a floating-point result; integer division in C never produces a float without casting or using float literals.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "2". "2" is correct because integer division 5/2 = 2 with remainder 1 discarded; %d prints 2.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "3". "3" sounds plausible but is wrong because 3 would require rounding up (ceiling), but C integer division truncates down.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "0". "0" sounds plausible but is wrong because 0 would imply 2/5 or a modulo confusion, not 5/2.

3.overview: Python identifier rules: must start with a letter or underscore; may contain letters, digits, and underscores; cannot start with a digit; hyphens and # are operators/syntax, not name characters. variable_1 satisfies all rules.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "1variable". "1variable" sounds plausible but is wrong because identifiers cannot begin with a digit — SyntaxError at parse time.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "variable_1". "variable_1" is correct because starts with letter, contains underscore and digit — fully valid Python name.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "variable-1". "variable-1" sounds plausible but is wrong because hyphen is the subtraction operator; Python parses this as variable minus 1.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "variable#1". "variable#1" sounds plausible but is wrong because # starts an inline comment; not part of an identifier.

3.studyTip: Python names: [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]* — no hyphens, no leading digits.

4.overview: break immediately terminates the innermost enclosing loop or switch, transferring control to the statement after the loop. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next loop test. They are frequently confused on exams.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Skips the current iteration". "Skips the current iteration" sounds plausible but is wrong because that is continue, not break — continue goes to next iteration while staying inside the loop.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Exits the loop entirely". "Exits the loop entirely" is correct because break leaves the loop completely; no further iterations run.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Restarts the loop". "Restarts the loop" sounds plausible but is wrong because no standard keyword restarts from iteration 1; you'd reassign counter or use a nested loop structure.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Continues to the next iteration". "Continues to the next iteration" sounds plausible but is wrong because that describes continue; break exits, not advances.

4.studyTip: break = exit loop; continue = skip to next iteration.

5.overview: Java constants are declared with final — applied to variables, methods (no override), or classes (no subclass). C/C++ use const; Python has no true const keyword; immutable is a general concept, not a Java keyword.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "static". "static" sounds plausible but is wrong because static means class-level membership/shared state, not immutability.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "final". "final" is correct because final variable must be assigned once; reference cannot point to new object (object internals may still mutate unless deeply immutable).
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "const". "const" sounds plausible but is wrong because const is C/C++ keyword; Java uses final instead.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "immutable". "immutable" sounds plausible but is wrong because not a Java keyword — immutability is achieved via final + design (e.g., String class).

5.studyTip: Java constant field: private static final TYPE NAME = value;

6.overview: Linear search scans each of n elements once in the worst case, comparing the target with every item until found or exhausted. Time complexity is O(n) — linear in input size. O(1) is direct index access; O(log n) is binary search on sorted data; O(n²) is nested loops.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(1)". "O(1)" sounds plausible but is wrong because constant time requires direct addressing (array index, hash lookup average case) — linear search may scan all n elements.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "O(n)". "O(n)" is correct because one pass through up to n elements → linear time.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "O(log n)". "O(log n)" sounds plausible but is wrong because logarithmic search halves the search space each step (binary search), not sequential scan.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "O(n²)". "O(n²)" sounds plausible but is wrong because quadratic time implies nested iteration over n — not a single linear scan.

6.studyTip: Unsorted search = O(n); sorted array binary search = O(log n).

7.overview: Conditional execution selects one path based on a Boolean condition. if-else (and switch/match variants) implement branching. Loops repeat; functions organize code; arrays store data.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Loop". "Loop" sounds plausible but is wrong because loops repeat while/for a condition; they don't choose between alternate single-pass paths like if-else.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Function". "Function" sounds plausible but is wrong because functions encapsulate code but don't inherently branch — branching uses if inside functions.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "If-else statement". "If-else statement" is correct because evaluates condition and executes exactly one branch — core conditional construct.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Array". "Array" sounds plausible but is wrong because arrays are data structures for storing multiple values, not control flow.

7.studyTip: Selection (if) vs iteration (loop) vs sequence (statements) — classic control-flow trio.

8.overview: Python comparison operators return bool. x > 5 is True (10>5) and x < 15 is True (10<15). and requires both True → print outputs True. It does not print the number 10 or raise an error.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "True". "True" is correct because both comparisons hold for x=10, so boolean and is True.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "False". "False" sounds plausible but is wrong because would require at least one comparison to fail — neither does for x=10.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "10". "10" sounds plausible but is wrong because print receives a boolean expression result, not the integer x.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Error". "Error" sounds plausible but is wrong because syntax and types are valid; no exception raised.

8.studyTip: Python print(bool_expr) prints True/False, not the original integer.

9.overview: C primitive types include int, char, float, double, void, etc. string is NOT a built-in primitive — C uses char arrays or char* for text. stdio.h provides string handling via C strings, not a string type.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "int". "int" sounds plausible but is wrong because int is fundamental numeric primitive in C.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "float". "float" sounds plausible but is wrong because float is standard floating-point primitive.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "string". "string" is correct because C has no string primitive; text is char[] or pointer to char.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "char". "char" sounds plausible but is wrong because char stores single character — primitive type.

9.studyTip: C primitives: int, char, float, double. Text = char array.

10.overview: Modular programming decomposes a large program into smaller modules (functions, classes, files) with clear interfaces. Benefits: easier testing, maintenance, team parallel work, and reuse. It does not eliminate debugging or intentionally slow execution.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "To increase code complexity". "To increase code complexity" sounds plausible but is wrong because modularity reduces perceived complexity by separation of concerns — opposite of this answer.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "To break a program into smaller, manageable functions". "To break a program into smaller, manageable functions" is correct because core definition of modular design — divide and conquer at code level.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "To eliminate the need for debugging". "To eliminate the need for debugging" sounds plausible but is wrong because bugs still occur; modules make isolation easier but don't remove debugging.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "To reduce program execution speed". "To reduce program execution speed" sounds plausible but is wrong because modularity may add tiny call overhead but goal is maintainability, not slower execution.

10.studyTip: Modular = smaller units + interfaces; think functions, packages, layers.

11.overview: Python supports tuple unpacking for simultaneous assignment: a, b = b, a swaps without temp variable by evaluating RHS tuple first then binding names. Arithmetic swap works in some languages but is unnecessary in Python. a=b; b=a fails to swap (loses original a). swap() is not built-in.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b". "a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b" sounds plausible but is wrong because arithmetic swap works in languages without tuple unpacking but is error-prone with overflow; Python idiomatic way is C.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "a = b; b = a". "a = b; b = a" sounds plausible but is wrong because after first line both hold b's old value — original a is lost.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "a, b = b, a". "a, b = b, a" is correct because Python evaluates (b, a) tuple then unpacks — elegant one-line swap.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "swap(a, b)". "swap(a, b)" sounds plausible but is wrong because no built-in swap(); you'd need a custom function.

11.studyTip: Python swap idiom: a, b = b, a — always remember RHS evaluated first.

12.overview: Arrays have fixed size (in many languages) and O(1) random access but costly insert/delete in middle. Linked lists allocate nodes dynamically — grow/shrink at runtime without predeclaring max size. Access is O(n) for linked lists; memory overhead per node exists.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Faster access time". "Faster access time" sounds plausible but is wrong because arrays offer O(1) index access; linked lists require O(n) traversal.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Dynamic size adjustment". "Dynamic size adjustment" is correct because linked lists allocate nodes as needed — primary advantage over static arrays.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Less memory usage". "Less memory usage" sounds plausible but is wrong because linked lists store pointer overhead per node — often MORE memory.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Constant-time insertion". "Constant-time insertion" sounds plausible but is wrong because insertion is O(1) only at known position with pointer; searching that position is still O(n).

12.studyTip: Linked list wins on dynamic size; array wins on random access.

13.overview: Stack: Last-In-First-Out — push adds to top, pop removes top (like plate stack). Queue: FIFO — first in, first out. Linked list is implementation structure; binary tree is hierarchical.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Queue". "Queue" sounds plausible but is wrong because queue is FIFO — opposite order of LIFO.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Stack". "Stack" is correct because LIFO defines stack behavior — used in call stacks, undo, parsing.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Linked List". "Linked List" sounds plausible but is wrong because linked list is implementation technique; LIFO describes stack ADT.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Binary Tree". "Binary Tree" sounds plausible but is wrong because tree organizes hierarchical data with left/right children, not LIFO.

13.studyTip: LIFO = Stack; FIFO = Queue — memorize both acronyms.

14.overview: QuickSort average O(n log n) but worst case O(n²) when pivots are poorly chosen (already sorted with first-element pivot). MergeSort guarantees O(n log n) worst case. Exam asks worst case.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(n log n)". "O(n log n)" sounds plausible but is wrong because average/good-case QuickSort, not worst case.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "O(n²)". "O(n²)" is correct because worst case with unbalanced partitions — all elements on one side of pivot.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "O(n)". "O(n)" sounds plausible but is wrong because linear time is one pass — QuickSort is divide-and-conquer with recursion.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "O(log n)". "O(log n)" sounds plausible but is wrong because logarithmic is binary search style, not sorting entire array.

14.studyTip: QuickSort worst = O(n²); MergeSort worst = O(n log n).

15.overview: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source to all vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edge weights. DFS/BFS don't handle weighted shortest path optimally. Merge Sort sorts arrays.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Depth-First Search". "Depth-First Search" sounds plausible but is wrong because DFS explores deeply — doesn't guarantee shortest weighted path.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Breadth-First Search". "Breadth-First Search" sounds plausible but is wrong because BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs, not weighted.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Dijkstra's Algorithm". "Dijkstra's Algorithm" is correct because classic greedy algorithm for non-negative weighted shortest paths.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Merge Sort". "Merge Sort" sounds plausible but is wrong because sorting algorithm, unrelated to graph pathfinding.

15.studyTip: Weighted shortest path (non-negative) → Dijkstra; unweighted → BFS.

16.overview: Binary Search Tree property: for every node, all keys in left subtree are less than node's key; all keys in right subtree are greater (or equal depending on variant). Less-than values go LEFT of root.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Right subtree". "Right subtree" sounds plausible but is wrong because right subtree holds values GREATER than root.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Left subtree". "Left subtree" is correct because BST invariant: left < root < right.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "Parent node". "Parent node" sounds plausible but is wrong because parent is one level up — not where all smaller values live.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Root node". "Root node" sounds plausible but is wrong because root is single comparison point; smaller values descend left.

16.studyTip: BST: left smaller, right larger — trace insertions on paper.

17.overview: Balanced BST (AVL, Red-Black) maintains height O(log n), so insert/search/delete are O(log n). Unbalanced degenerate tree can be O(n). Balanced guarantees logarithmic height.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "O(1)". "O(1)" sounds plausible but is wrong because insertion must traverse tree height — cannot be constant for arbitrary size.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "O(n)". "O(n)" sounds plausible but is wrong because would be skewed/unbalanced tree worst case, not balanced BST.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "O(log n)". "O(log n)" is correct because balanced tree height ~ log n → insert takes proportional steps.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "O(n²)". "O(n²)" sounds plausible but is wrong because no standard BST operation is quadratic for single insert.

17.studyTip: Balanced BST operations: O(log n); skewed chain: O(n).

18.overview: Inheritance allows subclass (derived) to acquire fields and methods from superclass (base). Encapsulation hides internals; polymorphism is many forms; abstraction hides complexity.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "Encapsulation". "Encapsulation" sounds plausible but is wrong because bundling data + methods with access control — not parent-child sharing.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "Polymorphism". "Polymorphism" sounds plausible but is wrong because same interface, different behavior — often uses inheritance but is distinct principle.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "Inheritance". "Inheritance" is correct because is-a relationship: Dog extends Animal inherits sound(), etc.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "Abstraction". "Abstraction" sounds plausible but is wrong because showing essential features while hiding detail — broader design concept.

18.studyTip: Four OOP pillars: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance, Polymorphism.

19.overview: Encapsulation restricts direct access to internal state via private fields and public getters/setters. Goal: protect invariants, reduce coupling, allow implementation change without breaking clients.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "To allow multiple inheritance". "To allow multiple inheritance" sounds plausible but is wrong because Java allows one class inheritance; multiple inheritance is separate language feature, not encapsulation's purpose.
options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "To hide data and restrict direct access". "To hide data and restrict direct access" is correct because private/protected modifiers + accessors = encapsulation.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "To enable method overloading". "To enable method overloading" sounds plausible but is wrong because overloading is compile-time polymorphism — same name, different parameters.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "To create abstract classes". "To create abstract classes" sounds plausible but is wrong because abstract classes support inheritance/abstraction, not primarily data hiding definition.

19.studyTip: Encapsulation = data hiding + controlled access through methods.

20.overview: Java this refers to current object instance — access instance fields, call other constructors (this()), pass current object. super refers to parent class. self is Python. instance is not keyword.

options.A: Option A (CORRECT): "this". "this" is correct because this.field, this.method(), this() constructor chaining.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "super". "super" sounds plausible but is wrong because super accesses superclass members — different from current object reference.
options.C: Option C (INCORRECT): "self". "self" sounds plausible but is wrong because Python convention for instance reference; Java uses this.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "instance". "instance" sounds plausible but is wrong because not a Java keyword for current object.

options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "No output". "No output" sounds plausible but is wrong because sound() explicitly prints Bark.

21.studyTip: Override + parent reference to child object → child method runs (dynamic binding).

options.B: Option B (CORRECT): "Overriding a method in a subclass". "Overriding a method in a subclass" is correct because runtime polymorphism through method override.

29.overview: Postfix x++ uses 5 then increments to 6. Prefix ++x increments first. Expression: x++ + ++x → 5 + 6 = 11? Wait: after x++ x becomes 6, ++x makes x=7 and uses 7? Trace: x=5; left x++ returns 5, x=6; ++x returns 7, x=7; 5+7=12. Answer is 12.

options.A: Option A (INCORRECT): "10". "10" sounds plausible but is wrong because would be 5+5 without prefix increment on second operand.
options.B: Option B (INCORRECT): "11". "11" sounds plausible but is wrong because common miscalculation ignoring that ++x increments before use.
options.C: Option C (CORRECT): "12". "12" is correct because x++ yields 5; ++x yields 7; sum = 12.
options.D: Option D (INCORRECT): "13". "13" sounds plausible but is wrong because over-counts increment steps.

29.studyTip: Trace increment operators left-to-right: postfix returns old, prefix returns new.
